extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in AI/computational creativity; narrative-generation system designers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging whether a narrative (machine- or human-produced) counts as genuinely creative according to the Lovelace Test and related computational-creativity principles. Focuses on thematic depth, character intentionality, causal coherence, reader effects, originality, and predictability/origination axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lovelace Test (original formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An artificial agent A passes the Lovelace Test iff A produces an output O such that: (1) A's designer cannot account for how A produced O; (2) A's design did not include O (it was not pre-programmed); (3) the output O is not the result of randomness or chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named for Ada Lovelace's claim that machines cannot 'originate' — the Test distinguishes mere generation from genuine origination. Intended as a diagnostic for when a machine truly originates; emphasizes epistemic unpredictability to the designer, absence of pre-programming of the output, and non-randomness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger Lovelace Test (Riedl 2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: A refinement: an output is creative if a human evaluator, knowing the system's design, judges the output to be both (a) of high value (well-formed, interesting) and (b) surprising relative to what the system was expected to produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts the criterion from designer-epistemic (can't account) to evaluator-based assessment of surprise plus value. Requires an informed human judge who understands the system's capabilities and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Intentionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must have explicit, inferable goals; events should arise from characters' intentional actions rather than happenstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRUTUS operationalizes this as a necessary storytelling feature: model characters' goals and intentions so that actions and plot developments are explainable as goal-directed behavior. Anti-patterns: characters as mere plot devices with no internal motivations; events that occur without agent-driven causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic Concept Structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex themes (e.g., betrayal, redemption, coming-of-age) must be instantiated via formal conceptual structures — e.g., modeling trust, expectation, and violation for 'betrayal'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRUTUS emphasizes explicit, formal modeling of thematic concepts rather than surface-level mentions of theme. Guidance: represent the conceptual elements and relations that make a theme meaningful so that plot and character behavior genuinely instantiate the theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-Targeted Effects / Engagement Scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should be calibrated to produce specific effects in a reader (surprise, sympathy, dread); the system should reason about what will surprise, satisfy, or move readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRUTUS includes reasoning about reader response as part of story construction. Evaluate whether the narrative scaffolds (pacing, revelation, emotional beats) are intentionally designed to elicit targeted responses. Anti-patterns: technically coherent stories that fail to engage or evoke intended emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine Thematic Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: The story must instantiate a complex theme rather than merely chronicle events or produce surface plot points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether theme is woven into character motivations, causal structure, and outcomes rather than appended as label. Examples: a betrayal theme should be demonstrably grounded in trust relations, expectations, and violations rather than a single explicit sentence naming 'betrayal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal Causal Coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Events follow logically from prior conditions and character intentions; plot causation is intelligible and consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate causal chains and whether outcomes are traceable to earlier states/intentions. Look for logical gaps, deus ex machina, or contrived coincidences. This criterion separates mere randomness from meaningful narrative causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (not predictable recombination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The output is not merely a recombination of templates or predictable components — it produces something its components do not predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the story goes beyond recombining learned templates or patterns: does it yield configurations, twists, or thematic instantiations that were not foreseeable given the system's parts? Related to Lovelace condition that output was not pre-programmed and not explainable by designer; also watch for plagiarism or template plumbing as failure modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability vs. Genuine Origination axis
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluative axis distinguishing competent but predictable generation from genuine origination; a story can be well-constructed yet fail the Lovelace sense of creativity if it matches expectations given the creator's prior work or design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this axis to compare expected output (given knowledge of the system/author) versus actual output. High craftsmanship + high predictability = competent but not Lovelace-creative. Genuine origination requires surprising deviation from expected patterns while maintaining value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise relative to prior knowledge (designer/author/readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is more creative if it would surprise even those familiar with the creator's prior work or the system's expected output (the 'Lovelace move' applied to human authorship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures both the original Lovelace emphasis (designer cannot account) and Riedl's evaluator-based surprise: assess surprise relative to knowledgeable observers (designer, prior readers, or evaluators who know the system). Surprise must be paired with value (not random oddity) to count as creativity.
